blocks.content: A Docker image is a read-only template that bundles your application code, its runtime, its dependencies, and instructions for how to run it, into one immutable artifact. Every container you have ever run started from one of these.

Images are not written by hand, they are built by running docker build against a Dockerfile, a plain text file listing the steps needed to assemble the environment (covered in full in the Dockerfile module). The output of that build process is the image itself.

blocks.alt: A Dockerfile is the recipe, the image is the result

blocks.content: Once built, an image never changes. When you run a container from it, Docker adds one thin, writable layer on top for that specific container's runtime changes, but the image underneath stays exactly as it was built. This is what makes it safe to start ten containers from the same image at once, none of them can corrupt what the others are reading from.

blocks.alt: The image stays frozen, only the container layer changes

blocks.content: Every image has two identities at once: a human-friendly repository:tag (like myapp:1.0) for you to type, and a unique, content-derived image ID (a sha256 hash) that Docker actually uses internally. Two different tags can point at the exact same image ID.

blocks.alt: A friendly name on the outside, a content hash underneath

blocks.content:
docker images
# REPOSITORY   TAG    IMAGE ID       SIZE
# myapp        1.0    9f2a1b3c4d5e   187MB

code.content:

# REPOSITORY   TAG    IMAGE ID       SIZE

# REPOSITORY   TAG    IMAGE ID       SIZE

blocks.content: Because the image is just a read-only template, it can back any number of independent, simultaneously running containers, each with its own writable layer, its own process, and its own lifecycle, all reading from the same underlying image data.

blocks.alt: The same template, many independent containers

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: An image is an immutable, read-only template built from a Dockerfile, a container is what you get when you actually run one.
Images have both a human-readable tag and a content-based image ID, and many tags can point at the exact same underlying image.
